intro: Pachmann’s DB 860 side begins with the F-major Étude, Op. 25 No. 3, before the C-sharp-minor Waltz. Both pieces remain in the original file; the comparison starts at the waltz’s later entry rather than silently removing the étude. A contemporary December 1925 review establishes that this side was already published.
question: How does Pachmann compress a waltz on a shared disc side?

cues.title: The first piece is an étude
cues.text: This is the complete HMV DB 860 side 2, not an isolated waltz file. Alan Kelly’s matrix discography identifies Op. 25 No. 3 followed by Op. 64 No. 2 on Cc6260-1.

cues.title: The waltz enters
cues.text: The quieter end of the étude gives way to the waltz around this point. The comparison map uses absolute times in this original stream, so its opening is not at the file’s zero.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/chopin-waltz-op64-2-pachmann-1925.txt: low-level region110–115 seconds; strong novelty118 seconds and C-sharp-minor region from 120 seconds Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: The waltz changes colour
cues.text: The analysis finds a change around 2:44 within the waltz. Follow the continuity of its line rather than treating the earlier étude as part of the same formal design.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/chopin-waltz-op64-2-pachmann-1925.txt: novelty164 seconds; the first117 seconds belong to another work Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: A later local crest
cues.text: This is one of the side’s highest average-level windows after the waltz has begun. The louder early windows belong to the preceding étude and must not be used as the waltz’s climax.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/chopin-waltz-op64-2-pachmann-1925.txt: high level185 seconds; global highest60 seconds belongs to Étude Op25/3 Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

cues.title: The shared side closes
cues.text: A final measured change precedes the quiet end of the side. Keep the phrase and its remaining resonance together, but do not count the étude’s time when comparing waltz durations.
cues.evidence: cache/analysis/chopin-waltz-op64-2-pachmann-1925.txt: novelty262 seconds; quiet late windows265–275 seconds Five-second level windows and two-second novelty estimates do not locate individual notes or prove a pedalling choice.

facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
